observations.label: brief-active
observations.output: Think of a cache like a sticky note with a shortcut. Cache invalidation is the process of sticking a new note on top so the old one doesn't get used anymore. It just tells the system to stop relying on that outdated data and instead fetch the fresh version.

observations.label: detailed-active
observations.output:
Cache invalidation is the process of telling a system that its stored, or "cached," data is no longer accurate and needs to be refetched from the original source. Imagine a web page stored locally to load faster; if the original server updates that page, the local copy becomes stale. Invalidation is the signal that triggers the system to discard that old copy and retrieve the new one, ensuring users see current information.

In practice, systems often use expiration times, where cached data is automatically considered invalid after a set period (Time-To-Live). Alternatively, event-driven invalidation explicitly purges specific items when their source data changes, such as when a user updates a profile. This balances performance by avoiding constant server hits while maintaining data accuracy through scheduled or reactive updates.
